title: The in vitro effect of omentin-1 on the global proteome of granulosa cells from normal weight Large White and fat Meishan pigs
projectDescription:
Granulosa cells (Gc) in the ovary play a vital role in nurturing oocyte development, producing estrogens, and maintaining the hormonal balance necessary for follicle maturation and successful ovulation. Omentin-1 (ITLN1) is an adipokine involved in energy metabolism and insulin resistance; its expression has been demonstrated in the ovary and varies depending on the degree of pig fatness. However, its effect on the global proteome of Gc has not been previously investigated. It was hypothesized that ITLN1 affects the abundance of proteins involved in key processes occurring in Gc during the mid-luteal phase of the estrous cycle in normal weight Large White and fat Meishan pigs, with potential variation based on the fat content of the pigs. Liquid chromatography‒tandem mass spectrometry (LC‒MS/MS) analysis of porcine Gc identified 208 statistically significant differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) in the Large White pigs, with 99 proteins upregulated, and 109 downregulated. In Meishan pigs, 42 statistically significant DAPs were identified, including 25 upregulated and 17 downregulated proteins. Western blotting and ELISA analyses of six selected DAPs (cadherin 5, farnesyl diphosphate synthase, fibroblast growth factor receptor 1, matrix metallopeptidase 2, phosphatidylinositol-5-phosphate 4-kinase type 2 gamma, and yes-associated protein 1) confirmed the accuracy and precision of the LC‒MS/MS methodology. The identified DAPs were associated with several key biological processes, including the estrogen signaling pathway, cell cycle and DNA replication, protein synthesis, transport and maturation, cytoskeleton dynamics, cell signaling, and hormonal regulation. The results indicate that ITLN1 has a modulatory influence on the porcine Gc proteome, which is dependent on fat content. This highlights the important role of ITLN1 in regulating ovarian functions.

sampleProcessingProtocol: The ovaries were obtained from sexually mature gilts of two breeds: normal weight Large White pigs and fat Meishan pigs. Following slaughter, the ovaries were promptly extracted and immersed in 0.1 M ice-cold phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, Thermo Fisher Scientific) containing antibiotics and transported to the laboratory for collection of medium follicles (4–6 mm in diameter; days 10–12 of the estrous cycle). In each experiment, ovarian follicle cells were obtained from four distinct animals (n = 4). The Gc cultures were prepared in accordance with the methodology outlined previously [Stoklosowa et al., 1982], with certain adaptations.  Protein isolation was performed using a cell lysis buffer containing 30 mM Tris–HCl (pH 8), 8 M urea, and 2% 3-[(3-cholamidopropyl)dimethylammonio]-1-propanesulfonate. After discarding the media, cells were treated with lysis buffer (100–150 µL per well) and incubated on ice for 30 min. The lysates were subsequently collected and vortexed three times for 15 s each. Next, the samples were incubated at 4°C for 45 min, and vortexing every 15 min. Then, the samples were centrifuged (10,000×g for 5 min at 4°C), and the supernatants were transferred to new sterile tubes. Protein concentrations were estimated via the Bradford assay. The samples were stored at -80°C. The samples were digested via a modified SP3 method with minor adjustments [Mielecki et al., 2023]. The resulting peptide solutions were transferred to new tubes, and the resin was further washed with 40 µL of 1% dimethyl sulfoxide in water, followed by 60 µL of water. Peptide concentrations from the pooled eluates were quantified via the Pierce Quantitative Colorimetric Peptide Assay. 15 µg of peptides in 110 µL of 100 mM TEAB buffer were labeled with TMTpro 16plex tags in 40 µL ACN for 1 h on a vortex. The reaction was quenched with 8 µL of 5% hydroxylamine. Peptides were combined and desalted via 30 mg Oasis HLB columns.  The mixed labeled peptides were separated via high-pH reverse-phase chromatography (HpRP) on an XBridge Peptide BEH C18 column (4.6 × 250 mm, 130 Å, 5 µm). The separation process was conducted at a flow rate of 0.8 mL/min over a 50-min period on a Waters Acquity UPLC H-class system. The mobile phases employed included water (A), ACN (B), and 100 mM ammonium hydroxide (C), with phase C maintained at a constant 10% throughout the gradient. Fraction collection commenced at the 2-min mark, with one fraction collected every min. The gradient schedule was as follows: solvent B was increased from 3% to 8% over the first 2 min, from 8% to 15% over the next 8 min, from 15% to 25% over the following 17 min, from 25% to 33% over 8 min, from 33% to 50% over 7 min, and then increased to 90% over 4.5 min. This was followed by a 1.5-min isocratic hold at 90% and final equilibration at 3% solvent B for 2 min. In total, 48 fractions were collected, dried via a SpeedVac, and reconstituted in Evosep solvent A (0.1% FA in water) with 30 min of vortexing followed by sonication. Fractions 1--16 were pooled with fractions 33--48 by combining every 32nd fraction, whereas the middle fractions (17--32), were directly subjected to mass spectrometry analysis. The HpRP fractions were analyzed via an LC‒MS/MS system comprising an Evosep One instrument (Evosep Biosystems) directly coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The samples were loaded onto disposable Evotips Pure C18 trap columns (Evosep Biosystems) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Peptide separation was carried out on an analytical column (Dr. Maisch C18 AQ, 1.9 µm beads, 150 µm ID, 15 cm length, Bruker) at a flow rate of 220 nL/min over 88 min via the Evosep Extended method (15 samples per day). Data acquisition was performed in positive ion mode with a data-dependent acquisition method. The MS1 resolution was set to 60,000, with a normalized automatic gain control (AGC) target of 300%, an automatic maximum injection time, and a scan range of 300--1700 m/z. For MS2, the resolution was set at 30,000, with a standard normalized AGC target, an automatic maximum injection time, and the top 25 precursors within a 1.2 m/z isolation window selected for LC‒MS/MS analysis. Dynamic exclusion was applied for 20 s with a mass tolerance of ±10 ppm, a precursor intensity threshold of 5e3, and a precursor fit threshold of 70%. The precursors were fragmented in HCD mode with a normalized collision energy of 30%. The TurboTMT resolution mode was set to “TMTpro Reagents.” The spray voltage was set to 2.1 kV, the funnel retardation factor was 40, and the heated capillary temperature was 275°C.
dataProcessingProtocol: The raw data were processed with the MaxQuant/Andromeda suite (version 2.5) via the Sus scrofa reference proteome from UniProt (UP000008227, version 2021_01, one protein sequence per gene, 22788 sequences) supplemented with a contaminant database. The search parameters were as follows: enzyme – trypsin/P, fixed modifications – methylthio (C), variable modifications – oxidation (M), quantification – TMTpro 16-plex (corrected according to the Certificate of Analysis), max missed cleavages – 2. PSM and protein FDR, performed via the target/decoy strategy with a reversed database, were set to 0.01. Further data analysis was performed in Perseus (version 1.6.15). Proteins identified by site, proteins from the reverse database, and potential contaminants were filtered out. Proteins without at least 3 values in at least one group were filtered out, after which the signal was normalized to loading factors. Data were then log2-transformed, and missing values were replaced from a normal distribution. The batch effect correction were performed in the R environment (ver. 4.3.1) using the Limma package (ver. 3.54.0). A two-sample t-test was performed to identify proteins that were differentially expressed between the treatment and control groups. The results that met the cutoff values of p < 0.05 and a fold change ≤ -1.2 or ≥ 1.2 were selected for further analyses.
